questions.question: What is HIV?
questions.answer:
HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) is a virus that attacks the immune system, the part of the body that fights infection. Many people have no symptoms for years, so testing is the only way to know your HIV status for sure.

An HIV home test kit lets you test yourself in private. You use a small finger-prick of blood, and the test looks for antibodies to HIV-1 and HIV-2. Your result shows in around 15 minutes, with nothing to post to a lab.

questions.question: What are the main symptoms of HIV?
questions.answer:
Some people get a short, flu-like illness 2 to 6 weeks after getting HIV. Signs can include:

  • High temperature or fever
  • Sore throat
  • A red rash on the body
  • Feeling very tired, or aching muscles

After this, many people feel completely well for years. You cannot tell if you have HIV by how you feel, which is why testing matters.

questions.question: Is HIV treatable?
questions.answer: Yes. HIV treatment is free on the NHS. With treatment, people with HIV live long, healthy lives, and once the virus is undetectable they cannot pass it on to partners. The earlier you know, the better.

questions.question: Who should take an HIV test?
questions.answer: Anyone who is sexually active can get HIV. It is a good idea to test if you have had sex without a condom, have a new partner, have shared needles, or your partner has HIV. If you often have new partners, testing every 3 months is a good habit.

accordions.heading: What is HIV?
accordions.content:
HIV is a virus that affects the immune system. It can be passed on through sex without a condom and may cause no noticeable symptoms for a long time.

There is currently no cure for HIV, but treatment is highly effective and allows people living with HIV to live long, healthy lives.

accordions.heading: Is this for you?
accordions.content:
You don’t need to have symptoms to test. HIV can cause no noticeable symptoms.

It may be worth testing if:
accordions.after: Had a possible HIV exposure in the last 72 hours? Don’t wait for a test result. Contact a sexual health clinic or go to A&E as soon as possible and ask about PEP, medication that can help prevent HIV after exposure.
checklist: You have a new sexual partner or more than one partner
A sexual partner has told you they have HIV or another STI
You have possible symptoms, such as a flu-like illness

benefits.text: Everything you need to test for HIV at home:

how.heading: How does the test work?
how.intro:
The test looks for antibodies your body can produce in response to HIV-1 or HIV-2 infection, using a small finger-prick blood sample.

Your result appears on the test pad in around 15 minutes, with no sample to send to a laboratory.

steps.title: Prick your finger
steps.text: Wash your hands and clean your fingertip with an alcohol pad. Let it dry, then use the lancet to prick your finger and form a drop of blood.

steps.title: Add blood and diluent
steps.text: Use the pipette to collect your blood and add 1 drop to the sample well marked S on the test pad. Then add 4 drops of diluent (test liquid) to the same well, immediately after the blood.

steps.title: Read your result
steps.text: Leave the test pad flat and read your result between 15 and 20 minutes. Don't read the test after 20 minutes, as the result may no longer be reliable.

windows.heading: When should I test?
windows.subheading: Testing too early can give a negative result even if you have an infection.
windows.initialTitle: Test now. If negative, repeat in 90 days.

questions.question: How soon after sex can I test for HIV?
questions.answer: This HIV rapid test gives a conclusive result 90 days (12 weeks) after possible exposure. You can test from [4 weeks], and many people will show a result by then, but you should test again at 90 days to be sure. If you want an earlier answer, a lab test at a sexual health clinic can detect HIV from around 45 days.

questions.question: It’s been less than 72 hours since I may have been exposed to HIV. What should I do?
questions.answer: Go to a sexual health clinic or A&E as soon as possible and ask about PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis). PEP is emergency medicine that can stop HIV infection. It must be started within 72 hours and works best within 24 hours. It’s too early to use a home test now, so test at 90 days.

questions.question: How accurate is the HIV rapid test?
questions.answer: This HIV home test is [99.x%] accurate when used correctly, 90 days or more after possible exposure. It’s CE marked for self-testing. Testing too early, or not following the instructions, can affect your result, so read the leaflet before you start.

questions.question: How do I use the HIV home test kit?
questions.answer: Wash and warm your hands, then use the lancet to prick the side of your fingertip. Add one drop of blood to the test, then add the liquid (diluent) from the kit. Wait 15 minutes and read your result. Everything you need is in the box, with step-by-step instructions.

questions.question: How do I read my HIV test result?
questions.answer: Look at the lines on the test after 15 minutes. One line at C means negative. Two lines (C and T) means positive, even if the T line is faint. If no line appears at C, the test is invalid and didn’t work, often because there wasn’t enough blood. Use a new test.

questions.question: What does a negative HIV test result mean?
questions.answer: A negative result means no HIV antibodies were found. If it has been 90 days or more since your last possible exposure, you can trust this result. If it has been less than 90 days, test again at the 90-day mark. Keep testing regularly if you’re sexually active.

questions.question: What if my HIV test result is positive?
questions.answer: A positive result means HIV antibodies may be present and needs a follow-up test to confirm it. Book a free, confidential appointment at a sexual health clinic or with your GP. Try not to panic: HIV is very treatable. With treatment, people live long, healthy lives and cannot pass HIV on to partners.

questions.question: Can I take an HIV test while pregnant?
questions.answer: Yes, you can use this HIV test while pregnant. [Check this against the kit leaflet.] In the UK, HIV testing is also offered free as part of routine antenatal care, so speak to your midwife too. If you are pregnant and have HIV, treatment makes the chance of passing it to your baby very low.

questions.question: Can I use this test if I take PrEP or HIV medicine?
questions.answer: This test isn’t suitable if you take PrEP, PEP or HIV treatment, because these medicines can affect the result. If you take PrEP, your sexual health clinic will give you regular HIV tests as part of your care. [Check this against the kit leaflet.]

questions.question: How fast is delivery, and is the packaging discreet?
questions.answer: We dispatch orders within 1 working day, and most arrive within 2 to 3 working days across the UK. Your HIV test kit arrives in a plain parcel with nothing on the outside to show what’s inside. Your bank statement won’t show “Test Discreet” or the name of the test, so your order stays private.

questions.question: Can I get a free HIV test on the NHS?
questions.answer: Yes. HIV tests are free at NHS sexual health clinics, and some areas offer free postal kits. Many people choose to buy a rapid HIV test instead, because it gives a result in 15 minutes at home, with no appointment, no forms and no sample to post to a lab.

questions.question: Does this test check for other STIs?
questions.answer: No, this kit only tests for HIV. If you may have been exposed to HIV, you may have been exposed to other STIs too, such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea or syphilis. Many STIs have no symptoms. Our 7-in-1 STI test bundle checks for several in one go.
